prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks to Katori and Ye, and I did not change my configuration between rounds. Round 1 left no scientific objection to the results themselves: the clocks have been compared at about 1e-18 by independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE), and gravitational redshift has been resolved over millimetre height differences. That is the independent confirmation I always ask for. The idea is distinct: magic-wavelength trapping lets many atoms be interrogated with the trap shift cancelled, which is a new clock architecture and not just a better ruler for optical frequencies. Katori proposed it and made the first strontium lattice clock; Ye's group showed the architecture could reach the lowest uncertainty and long coherence, and operated it in a regime where many-body effects are controlled. The two-name credit is the cleanest on the shortlist and sits comfortably inside the three-person limit. I also heed the chair's own caution: seven of eight round-1 positions converge on B052, but several members moved after reading colleagues, so I count it as one well-tested case, not seven independent votes. I put the case on the evidence and on the two AMO members' reading of the priority record, which I cannot check myself.
statement.case_against: The reservation that has not gone away is overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-trap prize, together with the view that this honours an instrument and not a discovery. The fundamental-physics payoff (drifting constants, ultralight dark matter) is still prospective, since no deviation has been seen, and the pending redefinition of the second has not happened. Olsson's statutory point is the sharpest: the prize is for the original discovery or invention, and Ye's role could be described as taking Katori's lattice clock to record performance. I judge that Ye's work is more than refinement, but I am an astroparticle experimentalist and rely on Lindroth, Kroll and Johansson for that. Attribution fringes remain (Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto, Yb, Hg and Al+ groups). If the committee decides that a discovery of nature must outrank a measurement technique, then B043 is where I would go, not B024.

responses.point: Olsson asks for evidence that Ye's contribution is original and decisive in its own right, not an improvement of Katori's invention, and notes that a Katori-only or differently composed citation would be more defensible if that cannot be shown.
responses.response: I cannot settle this from my own field, but I find the two-name split defensible on how the work developed. Katori holds the proposal and the first strontium lattice demonstration. The JILA programme then showed the architecture could operate with the lowest systematic uncertainty and coherence times far beyond the first demonstrations. That turned a proposal into the clock that other laboratories now compare against. I would not call that a mere refinement, since an invention that nobody can run at the claimed level is not yet a working clock. I would, however, draft the citation around the invention and the realisation of the lattice clock, and I would welcome Lindroth, Kroll or Johansson naming specific Ye-group results so the record shows what is his own and what belongs to Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and colleagues. A Katori-only prize would, in my view, understate the realisation. I would not support it unless the AMO members tell us that the JILA results are derivative.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B024), stressing the prediction-then-observation sequence and arguing that the existence of flat-band correlated phases does not depend on how the pairing question resolves, while conceding the Cao and earlier-theory attribution problem.
responses.response: I agree that the distinction between unsettled interpretation and unsettled discovery is a real one, and I withdraw nothing of my respect for the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 observations. Having read the full exchange, I have moved B024 up and now name it as my second alternative. What keeps it behind B052 this year is credit. You and Eriksson both accept that Cao, first author of the 2018 papers, and the earlier theorists fall outside the trio, and that two of the three places rest on one theory paper. A prize that the community will read as leaving out a decisive experimentalist is a larger risk than waiting. Condensed matter is outside my expertise, so I give weight to your and Eriksson's judgement of the physics, but on the attribution record I cannot support B024 as the first choice now.

responses.point: Danielsson now lists B052 first but keeps B010 and B043 as alternatives, and warns against letting the three-person statute decide what counts as important. He also questions whether the lattice clock is instrumentation before it is discovery.
responses.response: I agree that the three-person limit must not become the criterion of importance, and I would not use it that way for B052; the case rests on the physics and the clean credit happens to fit. On your question of discovery against instrument, my answer is that the Higgs observation is precisely the kind of discovery of nature we should recognise one day, but that is a separate matter from whether we can assign it fairly this year. On IceCube, you and Johansson are right that the diffuse flux is solid and the source associations (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane) are few and at moderate significance. I would add that the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND pioneers make the Halzen and Spiering pair contestable. I therefore keep B043 as a strong candidate for a later year and as my first alternative, not as a second part for this year.

responses.point: Kroll holds B052 first and B035 (atom interferometry) as an alternative, while noting that his and Lindroth's near-identical openings should not be double-counted and that the pending redefinition of the second is not a scientific criterion.
responses.response: I agree that your opening and Lindroth's should not be counted twice, and I have applied the same discount to the chair's own tally. I also agree that the redefinition of the second has not happened and should not enter our judgement. On a two-part prize with B035, I ask you directly: you and Lindroth both say the Chu absence and the Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich split make the trio contested, and I find that persuasive. A second part would add attribution risk for little scientific gain, since B052 already stands as a complete configuration. I have therefore dropped B035 from my alternatives.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B052 but asks whether the clock is precision engineering and not new physics, and whether Ye's possible later nuclear-clock credit should affect timing; his alternatives are the verified new states of matter in B021 and B024.
responses.response: I think your concern about timing is fair, and I would handle it with the citation rather than by delay. Wording that names the optical lattice clock and magic-wavelength trapping leaves the thorium-229 nuclear clock open for a future decision. I would also resist the idea that waiting improves the case: the lattice clock is as mature and as widely reproduced as anything on the shortlist. On your point about new states of matter, I agree that B021 and B024 are the strongest kind of discovery in principle. B021 I cannot support because Kane, Mele and Molenkamp leave out Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore and the three-dimensional work, as you yourself list.

uncertainties: Whether the AMO members can identify specific Ye-group results that are original and decisive, to meet Olsson's statutory objection; I cannot verify the priority record myself.
Whether lattice clocks are sufficiently distinct in discovery terms from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-trap prize; I believe so but it is a judgement.
Whether Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto or ion-clock pioneers have claims strong enough to change the two-name credit.
Whether a later nuclear-clock prize would overlap with this citation if the wording is too broad.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with Katori or Ye: I have no recorded connection to either or their institutions. For B043 (IceCube) and B041 (EHT) I am in the same broad experimental astroparticle and astrophysics community, with no collaboration with those teams; my work is in PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur. B043 is only an alternative, but I would recuse myself from chairing the discussion on it if it became live. As Chair I run the process, and I have tried to keep my own configuration based on the scientific record and not on counts of supporters.
